{{also|Ketchup|kétchup}}
==English==
{{wp}}
[[File:Organic Heinz Tomato Ketchup.jpg|thumb|A bottle of tomato '''ketchup'''.]]
[[File:Mushroom ketchup.jpg|thumb|A bottle of mushroom '''ketchup'''.]]

===Alternative forms===
* {{alt|en|catchup|catsup|katsup}}
* {{alt|en|katjap|kechap|ketsup||all|_|obsolete}}

===Etymology===
{{ety|en|:bor<unc>|ms:kecap<id:sauce>|tree=+}}
{{unc|en}}, but probably ultimately from {{der|en|nan-hbl|膎汁|tr=kê-chiap|t=[[fish sauce]]|lit=[[pickled]] [[fish]] [[juice]]}}, via {{bor|en|ms|kecap//kicap|t= any dark clear sauce from soybeans, fish, etc.}}, though the precise path is unclear – there are related words in various Chinese languages. Various other theories exist – see [[w:Ketchup#Etymology|Ketchup: Etymology]] for extended discussion.

First appeared in English in the late 17th century in reference to a Southeast Asian sauce encountered by British traders and sailors. The ''Oxford English Dictionary'' notes that it was commonly used in the 18th century to refer to a variety of similar sauces with varying ingredients—"anchovies, mushrooms, walnuts, and oysters being particularly popular"—but by the late 19th century the current tomato ketchup became the most popular form.<ref>"Ketchup", ''Oxford English Dictionary'' (online edition, 2020).</ref>

{{m|en|catsup|Catsup}} (earlier {{m|en|catchup}}) is an alternative Anglicization, still in use in the U.S., though it is now somewhat rare.

** {{audio|en|En-us-ketchup.ogg|a=US}}
** {{audio|en|En-ketchup.ogg|a=Canada}}
* {{IPA|en|/ˈkɛt͡ʃ.ʊp/|a=Northern England}}
* {{hmp|en|catch-up}} {{q|one pronunciation}}

===Noun===
{{en-noun|~}}

# {{lb|en|uncountable|chiefly|US|Canada|UK}} {{ellipsis of|en|tomato ketchup|t=a [[tomato]]-[[vinegar]]-based [[sauce]], sometimes containing [[spice]]s, [[onion]] or [[garlic]], and (especially in the US) [[sweetener]]s}}.
#: {{syn|en|tomato catsup}}
#: {{hyper|en|tomato sauce|red ketchup|red catsup}}
#: {{ux|en|tomato '''ketchup'''}}
#: {{ux|en|This diner serves '''ketchup''' in red bottles, and mustard in yellow ones.}}
# {{lb|en|countable|now|rare}} Such a sauce more generally (not necessarily based on tomatoes, but with mushrooms, fish, etc.). This is the older meaning.
#: {{hypo|en|tomato ketchup|tomato catsup|fruit ketchup|fruit catsup|corn ketchup|corn catsup|green ketchup|green catsup|yellow ketchup|yellow catsup}}
#* {{quote-book|en|year=1883|title=Cassell's Dictionary of Cookery|page=lxxxiii|text=The bottles, however, were port bottles, but contained mushroom '''ketchup'''; {{...}}}}
#* {{quote-book|en|year=2003|title=Inns and Bed and Breakfasts in Quebec 2003|publisher=Ulysses Travel Guides|page=46|text=To accompany meat, we prepare fruit '''ketchups''' and rhubarb chutney.}}

====Usage notes====
* The spelling ''ketchup'' became significantly preferred in the United States due to the popularity of the {{w|Heinz Tomato Ketchup|Heinz}} brand, which shortly after its introduction in 1876 switched from {{m|en|catsup}} to this spelling to distinguish itself from competitors. Other major brands, such as Hunt, subsequently followed, with Del Monte only switching to ''ketchup'' in 1988.<ref>“[http://www.slate.com/blogs/browbeat/2013/04/22/ketchup_vs_catsup_differences_none_at_all_video.html Is There a Difference Between Ketchup and Catsup?]”, ''Slate,'' Aisha Harris, April 22, 2013</ref>

* This condiment is more commonly and somewhat ambiguously called {{m|en|tomato sauce}} outside of North America and the United Kingdom. In South Africa, the word ''ketchup'' is not generally understood.
